confidence_note: Checked against the book text (Introduction). The old reference example (buying a swing vs planting a tree in a playground) and the company/stress examples are not in the book and are dropped. The Slinky demonstration is Meadows's own classroom routine, told in the first person in the book; the students' answer is quoted in the book.
facts: In Thinking in Systems, Donella Meadows describes a demonstration she used early on when teaching: she perches a Slinky on one upturned palm and grasps it from the top with the fingers of the other hand.
She pulls the bottom hand away. The lower end of the Slinky drops, bounces back up and yo-yos, hanging from her fingers.
She asks what made it bounce. The students answer: 'Your hand. You took away your hand.'
She then takes the box the Slinky came in, holds it the same way and pulls the lower hand away with as much drama as she can. Nothing happens; the box just hangs there.
The answer lies within the Slinky itself: the hands only suppress or release behavior latent in the structure of the spring. She calls this a central insight of systems theory.
She writes that the system, to a large extent, causes its own behavior; an outside event may unleash it, but the same event on a different system will likely give a different result.

Her examples: competitors rarely cause a company to lose market share; the company creates its losses at least in part through its own policies. The flu virus does not attack you; you set up the conditions for it to flourish.

Other examples she gives: political leaders don't cause recessions or economic booms; ups and downs are inherent in the structure of the market economy. Her definition: a system is a set of things, people, cells, molecules, interconnected so that they produce their own pattern of behavior over time. Oil-exporting nations are not solely responsible for oil-price rises: the importing nations' own consumption, pricing and investment policies built economies vulnerable to supply interruptions.
scene_details: a Slinky perched on an upturned palm
the spring yo-yoing from her fingers
the empty Slinky box hanging motionless
tension: Everyone in the room is sure the hand caused the bounce, until the same move on a box does nothing.
opening_idea: Start with the Slinky on her palm and the hand pulled away.

lessons.idea: When the same problem keeps coming back, look at the structure that produces it before blaming the latest trigger.
lessons.anchor: Same hand movement, Slinky bounces, box does not; the behavior is in the spring.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A family that argues every Sunday evening notices the fights always start when everyone is planning the week at once, and moves the planning to a calmer moment.

reflect_final: Which recurring problem in your work or home do you usually blame on the latest trigger rather than on how things are set up?

use_cases.situation: The team blames a competitor for lost customers.
use_cases.move: Mention Meadows's point that competitors rarely cause lost market share and ask which of our own policies might be doing it.

use_cases.situation: A colleague keeps getting blamed for missed deadlines.
use_cases.move: Ask together what in the workflow keeps producing the delay, before deciding who is at fault.

use_cases.situation: The same argument returns at home.
use_cases.move: Notice when and where it starts, and change that setting once before discussing who is right.

pocket_idea: Pull the hand away from a Slinky and it bounces, from a box nothing: look at the structure.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Meadows's students said her hand made the Slinky bounce, so she did the same with the empty box and nothing happened.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Slinky on palm, hand away, bounce, 'your hand', box test, nothing; behavior lies in the structure; competitors example.
